title: Object-Oriented Paradigm
relevance: Interviewers use OOP basics to check whether candidates can design maintainable code by bundling state with behavior instead of scattering shared data across free functions.

phases.goal: Establish what OOP is and how it differs from procedural programming.

must_hit.point: OOP is a paradigm based on objects that contain data (fields/attributes) and code (procedures/methods).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines objects as units holding both attributes and methods, not just data structs.

must_hit.point: In procedural programming, data and functions are completely separate entities; shared/global state becomes hard to manage as many functions touch the same data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says functions operate on separate data and that shared state causes unpredictable bugs when changed.

must_hit.point: OOP bundles data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit (an object), e.g. car.drive() instead of drive(car).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts free function over external data with a method on the object that owns the data.

must_hit.point: The four foundational principles are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four pillars; brief definitions are a plus but naming them is enough at this stage.

probes: How does OOP differ from procedural programming when organizing data and the code that uses it?
What are the four pillars of OOP at a high level?

hints.1: Think about whether data and the operations on it live apart or together.
hints.2: Contrast a free function like drive(car) with a car object that has a drive() method, then name the four classic OOP principles.
hints.3: OOP = objects with attributes + methods; procedural keeps data and functions separate; pillars are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.

phases.goal: Show how Python applies OOP uniformly: every value is an object with a class type and methods.

must_hit.point: In Python, every piece of data—numbers, strings, functions, and even classes—is an object with a type (a class) plus attributes and methods.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that values are class instances and carry behavior, not bare primitives.

must_hit.point: Even a literal like 5 is an instance of the int class (type(5) reports <class 'int'>), so OOP rules apply consistently across the language.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the int example or equivalent: simple values are class instances with methods.

must_hit.point: You can pass a function into another function the same way you pass an integer because both are objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions uniform treatment of functions and ints as first-class objects.

probes: In Python, is an integer a primitive, or an object? How would you show that?
If everything is an object, what does that imply about calling methods on numbers?

hints.1: Ask what type(5) returns and whether that type is a class.
hints.2: Recall that numbers, strings, functions, and classes are all objects with attributes/methods.
hints.3: 5 is an int instance; there are no Java/C-style primitives—you can call methods like (5).bit_length().

phases.goal: Clarify when bundling data with behavior helps versus when another paradigm fits better.

must_hit.point: OOP modularity (data + operations in one object) makes complex systems easier to design, scale, and maintain than sprawling procedural shared state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Argues maintainability/scalability benefits of encapsulating related data and methods.

must_hit.point: OOP is a poor fit for hyper-optimized, cache-friendly data processing (Data-Oriented Design is often better) or purely mathematical transformations (Functional Programming is better).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names DOD and/or FP as better alternatives for those respective cases.

probes: When would you prefer procedural or another paradigm over OOP?
What problem does OOP solve relative to procedural code with lots of shared data?

hints.1: Consider maintainability of shared state versus raw performance or pure transforms.
hints.2: OOP helps design/scale/maintain by bundling data with methods; DOD and FP win in other niches.
hints.3: Prefer OOP for modular maintainable systems; prefer Data-Oriented Design for cache-friendly bulk processing and Functional Programming for pure mathematical transformations.

phases.goal: Apply the paradigm by placing related data and behavior on objects rather than free functions.

must_hit.point: A procedural salary helper is a free function over separate inputs (e.g. calculate_salary(base, bonus)); the OOP form keeps base/bonus on an Employee and exposes get_salary.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps the worked example: state on the object, method returns base + bonus.

must_hit.point: For a Bank-style design, Account should own its data and expose operations such as deposit (and related mutators like withdraw).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Puts balance/identity on Account and lists methods that mutate or query that state.

probes: Rewrite a procedural calculate_salary(base, bonus) in an OOP style.
What data and methods belong on an Account in a simple Bank system?

hints.1: Decide what lives on the object versus what stays as a standalone function.
hints.2: Move base/bonus onto Employee with get_salary; for Account, put balance (and id) on the object with deposit/withdraw-style methods.
hints.3: class Employee with get_salary using self.base + self.bonus; Account holds balance and methods like deposit and withdraw.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Procedural keeps data and functions separate, which is fine for simple scripts but shared/global state becomes unwieldy as many functions touch the same data; OOP bundles data with the functions that operate on it into objects for better modularity, scale, and maintenance.

tradeoffs.topic: OOP vs Data-Oriented Design / Functional Programming
tradeoffs.strong_answer: OOP breaks down for hyper-optimized, cache-friendly data processing (favor Data-Oriented Design) and for purely mathematical transformations (favor Functional Programming).

gotchas.trap: Treating Python ints/booleans as Java/C-style primitives that have no methods.
gotchas.correction: Python has no primitives in that sense; values like 5 are int instances and you can call methods such as (5).bit_length().

gotchas.trap: Keeping operations as free functions over external structures (drive(car)) when the behavior belongs with the data.
gotchas.correction: Model a car object that knows how to drive() itself so data and behavior stay together.
